title: A Letter to Your New Employee
author: Managing the Future
summary: The widely circulated "10 Things That Require Zero Talent" framework offers a reliable baseline for setting expectations with new employees because it names the behavioral commitments any organization can hold anyone to, regardless of background or skill level. Adapted here as a direct letter from manager to new employee, the framework covers ten commitments: punctuality, consistent work ethic, willingness to learn, passion for the outcome, energy, attitude management, coachability, doing a little extra, coming prepared, and putting the team first. Each is framed as a daily choice, not an innate quality, which explicitly reduces first-day anxiety while establishing clear standards. A letter like this serves three practical purposes in onboarding: it signals intentionality, creates a shared vocabulary for coaching and correction, and communicates that what matters most in the first ninety days is character and reliability rather than expertise. The author recommends making this letter a standard onboarding document alongside a personal User Manual, and notes that the same ten commitments apply equally to every level of leadership.
points: The ten commitments most predictive of early success require zero talent: punctuality, work ethic, openness to learning, caring about outcomes, energy, attitude management, coachability, exceeding what's asked, preparation, and putting the team first—each is a daily decision, not a fixed trait.

Framing early expectations as choices rather than skills reduces new-employee anxiety while creating a fair, legible baseline for coaching: the letter explicitly says it doesn't expect the new hire to be the most talented person in the room—just to show up and commit.

An explicit onboarding letter about behavioral standards does the relationship-building work before the first friction arises, establishing a shared frame for feedback and correction rather than waiting for an incident to surface unstated expectations.

Coachability—the ability to absorb criticism without losing motivation—is the most high-leverage item on the list and the one most often overlooked, because it is what separates people who grow throughout a career from those who plateau early.

The standards point upward as well as downward: the closing instruction reminds the manager that the same ten commitments they're asking from their newest hire apply to everyone on the team, at every level.
quotes: When you arrive on time—to work and to meetings—and when you meet your deadlines, you communicate to everyone around you that their time matters. When you don’t, you are telling them the opposite.
I will never ask you to be the most talented person in the room, but I will always expect you to be in the room when the meeting starts.

I ask that you do the work you committed to do at the standard you would want if the roles were reversed. Cutting corners may save you time, but that shortcut will then become one of your colleagues’ problem.
When you visibly care, the people around you try harder. When you visibly don’t, they notice that too.

The ability to absorb criticism without losing your motivation is what separates people who grow from people who plateau. If you can perform under pressure and stay open to correction, there is almost no limit to how far you can go in this organization.
Doing slightly more than what is required is a predictable way to earn trust here. Sometimes the “extra” is for the company. More often, it is for the person next to you who is having a hard day.

What is not on this list of expectations: intelligence, credentials, experience, natural gifts. We hired you in part because you have these things. But they are not what matters most in your first ninety days, nor are they what will determine your trajectory here.
